text: Thomas Eisner (June 25, 1929 – March 25, 2011) was a German-American entomologist and ecologist known as the "father of chemical ecology." He held the Jacob Gould Schurman Professorship in Chemical Ecology at Cornell University and served as director of the Cornell Institute for Research in Chemical Ecology (CIRCE). A world authority on animal behavior, ecology, and evolution, Eisner, along with his Cornell colleague Jerrold Meinwald, was a pioneer in chemical ecology, the study of chemical interactions among organisms. He authored or co-authored 400 scientific articles and seven books. Born in Berlin, Germany, on June 25, 1929, Eisner's father, Hans Eisner, was a Jewish chemist who worked with Fritz Haber at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Electrochemistry and later held a chemistry chair at Cornell; his mother, Margarete Heil-Eisner, was an artist. After escaping the Nazi regime, the family moved to Barcelona and then to Uruguay, before relocating to the United States in 1947. Eisner became a naturalized American citizen and, though rejected as an undergraduate at Cornell, earned his B.S. and PhD from Harvard University. He joined Cornell's entomology faculty in 1957 and married Maria Eisner, a member of his lab. In 1964, he helped establish the Department of Neurobiology and Behavior, where he worked until his death. A passionate nature photographer and videographer, Eisner's film *Secret Weapons* won the Grand Award at the New York Film Festival and was named Best Science Film by the British Association for the Advancement of Science. He was also an avid pianist and occasional conductor. Eisner died on March 25, 2011, from Parkinson's disease. He was an atheist. His primary research focused on chemical defenses in insects against predation, including his discovery that the bombardier beetle produces a chemical reaction to expel a boiling, noxious liquid from a nozzle in its abdomen. With field experience across four continents, Eisner was an active conservationist, serving on the boards of the National Audubon Society, the National Scientific Council of the Nature Conservancy, and the World Resources Institute Council. He was past president of the American Society of Naturalists and chairman of the Biology Section of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and played a key role in launching the Congressional Fellow Program in Washington, D.C., as well as in preserving wilderness areas in Florida and Texas. He was a member of the National Academy of Sciences, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the American Philosophical Society. Eisner received numerous honors, including the Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement, the Harvard Centennial Medal, the 1994 National Medal of Science, and the Lewis Thomas Prize for Writing about Science. He held honorary degrees from universities in Sweden, Germany, Switzerland, and the United States and was a foreign fellow of the Royal Society. He was also a member of the Deutsche Akademie der Naturforscher Leopoldina and Academia Europaea. In 2008, he was awarded the John J. Carty Award by the National Academy of Sciences.
